title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
The failure here is a model asserting fabricated information as fact. An AI legal research tool called Irys generated case citations, case titles, and quoted holdings that did not exist, and those invented references were submitted in court filings without being verified against actual legal databases. The failure occurred at the point of use, after the AI produced its output and before any human check confirmed whether the cited cases were real. Seven nonexistent citations appeared across eight separate filings before the problem was identified.

The attorney who used the tool believed it included accuracy checks, and it did not. That gap between the user's assumption about the system's capabilities and what the system actually did is where verification broke down. Catching this would have required manually confirming each citation against an authoritative legal database before filing, a step that was not taken.

What is not established is whether the tool itself was marketed as including verification, whether State Farm as a company had any direct role in the research process, or what sanctions, if any, will follow from the court.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized after using artificial intelligence that generated fake court cases, nonexistent quotes, and fictional legal holdings in court filings for a Los Angeles homeowner lawsuit. The case involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire made her Carson home uninhabitable. While repairs were underway, a storm caused water damage, and after delays in getting State Farm's approval, the work was never completed. Meni-Siliga and her husband exhausted their savings, filed for bankruptcy, and lost the home to foreclosure.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys thinking it would perform accuracy checks, but it did not. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel accepted responsibility for the filings. The case is scheduled for trial in October. State Farm's statement indicated the company expects its lawyers to maintain the highest ethical standards and confirm accuracy of all legal filings.
